title: Pog and Pip's Pebble Quest
markdown:
Pog the little goblin lived in a snug hollow under the roots of an old pine tree. His home was right by the Whispering Woods, a place he knew better than his own mossy hands. Pog didn’t dream of big adventures. He loved the quiet rustle of leaves, the smell of damp earth, and his best friend, Pip.

Pip was no ordinary friend. Pip was a bat, small and soft like velvet, with ears that twitched at every tiny sound. Pip’s favourite thing was napping in Pog’s pocket. Sometimes, he’d find a particularly cozy nook in Pog’s collection of shiny pebbles. Today, Pip needed a new napping spot, something extra-special. Pog had a plan. He wanted to find the most perfect, shiniest pebble in the whole wide world for Pip. That was his quest.

“Come on, Pip,” Pog whispered. His voice was as soft as a sigh of wind. Pip stirred and gave a sleepy chirp. Pog held out his hand. Pip fluttered his wings and landed on Pog’s wrist.

They walked along a familiar, rocky path. The smell of pine needles tickled Pog’s nose. The sun peeked through the branches of Owlglass Mountain, making dappled patterns on the forest floor. It was a perfect day for finding pebbles. Suddenly, a loud, odd sound floated towards them. It wasn’t the happy chirping of birds or the grumpy hoot of an owl. It sounded like arguing. Very loud, very muddled arguing.

Pog’s ears, usually quite good, flattened against his head. A tremor rippled through his mossy skin. A shiver, not of cold, but of worry, ran through him. Loud noises always made him feel wobbly. His paws felt clammy and slick against his wrist. His deepest fear was loud, unpredictable noises, and this sounded like a whole lot of both. He almost turned back. His heart thumped against his ribs like a trapped moth. Pip nudged his ear with his tiny nose. *Don’t worry,* Pip seemed to say. *I’m here.*

The arguing grew louder. It came from a small clearing just ahead, a place Pog had never explored. Pog took a deep breath. The smell of damp earth suddenly wasn’t so comforting. He really wanted to find Pip’s perfect pebble, but a feeling tugged him back. *Just a little peek, Pip,* he murmured. He crept towards the edge of the trees. His green toes sank softly into the moss.

In the clearing, two figures were indeed talking very loudly. One was Elara, a witch with a pointy hat that seemed to have a mind of its own. It tipped sideways, as if about to fall. She smelled of cinnamon and elderflower, a usually pleasant scent that seemed a bit sharp today. The other was Barnaby, a wizard whose glasses kept sliding down his nose. He pushed them back with an impatient flick. He smelled of old parchment and a hint of dried lavender.

“It’s *my* Moonpetal Dust!” Elara declared. Her voice was high and clear. She pointed a sapphire nail at a patch of disturbed earth. “I left it by the bubbling cauldron, right next to the toadstools!”

“Nonsense, Elara!” Barnaby huffed. He pushed his glasses up again. “That was *my* shimmer-root! I need it for my invisibility potion. You’ve misplaced it again, just like the griffin feather last Tuesday!”

Pog watched, his eyes wide with curiosity. He’d never seen a witch and a wizard argue before. They weren’t scary, not really. Just very loud. They stomped. Pebbles skittered. Hands waved like windmills. Voices boomed, echoing off the trees. Pog’s ears ached. He felt an urge to hide, to burrow into the earth until the noise stopped. He squeezed his eyes shut. The bright daylight felt too much. Pip gave a soft, encouraging chirp from his shoulder. It was a small sound in the din.

Then, Pog noticed something. Pip, usually so calm, was flapping his wings. His velvet head was tilted. His large ears swiveled. He was looking, not at the bickering humans, but at a low branch. A small, pale flower dangled there, its petals shimmering faintly in a sunbeam. Elara and Barnaby were so busy looking at each other, and at the ground, they hadn’t seen it.

“Um,” Pog began. His voice was a tiny squeak, barely heard above the shouting. He pointed a wobbly finger. His hand trembled a little. “Is… is that it?”

Elara and Barnaby stopped. They turned. Their eyes, wide with annoyance, followed Pog’s finger. Elara gasped. Her pointy hat wobbled. “My Moonpetal Dust!” Barnaby blinked. “Well, I’ll be… it *does* look remarkably like my shimmer-root ingredient, doesn’t it?”

A silence fell, heavier than any argument. The two magical folk looked at the flower, then at each other. Sheepish looks spread across their faces, like children caught with jam on their noses. Pog felt relief wash over him. It made his knees feel weak. The loud noises had stopped.

“Oh, dear,” Elara said. Her hat wobbled as she chuckled. It sounded like tinkling bells. “We were quite worked up, weren’t we? Making a dreadful fuss.”

“Indeed,” Barnaby admitted. He sighed, and all his pomposity seemed to float away. “My apologies, Elara. And yours, young… uh… goblin.”

Pog shuffled his feet. The soft moss cushioned his steps. Now, they were looking at *him*. A blush crept up his green cheeks. He wished he had a nice, shiny pebble to offer them, something smooth and reassuring to make things less awkward.

“It’s… Pog,” he managed. His voice was still quiet. “And this is Pip.”

Elara smiled. It was a warm, crinkly smile that reached her eyes. Her pointy hat settled a little. “Well, Pog and Pip, you’ve saved the day! We couldn’t find it anywhere. The invisibility potion would have been quite ruined without it.”

Barnaby nodded. There was respect in his voice. “A very clever find. Though, I suppose we owe you something for intervening in our little… disagreement. You were quite brave to speak up.” He looked at Pog, his gaze steady.

Pog’s mind raced. What could he give them? He didn’t have any shiny pebbles in his pockets. He did have a small pouch of his special dandelion sweets. They were his absolute favourite, made with sunshine-sweet honey and the finest dandelion fluff. He clutched the pouch. Its roughness felt familiar and comforting. Sharing them meant having fewer for himself, fewer to enjoy on quiet afternoons with Pip. He pictured the sweet, chewy goodness melting in his mouth. He imagined the sunshine-sweet honey, the delicate puff of dandelion fluff dissolving on his tongue, a moment of pure, quiet joy saved for just them. It was a small thing, this pouch of sweets, but for Pog, it felt like a big sacrifice. He pictured Pip’s happy chirps when he shared a sweet with him, the tiny flutter of wings as Pip nibbled a piece. That made it harder. He took another deep breath. The scent of pine needles was suddenly very reassuring.

He pictured Elara and Barnaby, no longer arguing, but perhaps sharing a chuckle over his simple offering. That made up his mind. “Here,” Pog said. He held out the pouch. The leather felt soft and yielding in his hand. “These are dandelion sweets. They’re very good. My Mum makes them.”

Elara and Barnaby looked at the pouch, then at each other, and then at Pog. Elara’s smile grew even warmer. “That’s very kind, Pog. Thank you. What a thoughtful gesture.” Barnaby nodded. A twinkle was in his eye that hadn’t been there before. “Indeed. A true act of generosity. Your Mum must be very proud.”

They each took a sweet. Their fingers brushed gently against Pog’s. To Pog’s surprise, they didn’t eat them right away. They carefully put them in their own pouches, securing them with a satisfied pat. “We shall savor these,” Barnaby said. His voice lost its earlier huffiness.

“Thank you, Pog,” Elara added. Her voice was softer now, like a gentle breeze. “You showed us a better way. Sometimes, you just need a little kindness to stop the bickering.”

Pog felt warmth spread through him, a feeling much nicer than the wobbly fear he’d felt earlier. He and Pip, with a friendly nod to the now much calmer witch and wizard, turned and made their way back along the rocky path. The arguing had stopped completely. A quiet, companionable murmur had taken its place, like two old friends reminiscing.

Back in his cozy hollow, Pog found the most perfect, smooth, grey pebble he had ever seen. It gleamed under the pine needles, cool and solid. He carefully placed it in Pip’s newly prepared napping hollow. Pip nudged it with his nose, chirped with delight, and promptly curled up, a small, velvety ball of happiness. Pog watched him. A contented sigh escaped his lips. The scent of pine needles was sweet and familiar.

Later that evening, as the stars began to prick the twilight sky, Pog heard a distant, happy hooo-hooo from an owl. It was a loud sound, a call across the darkening woods, but it no longer made Pog flinch. He realized that even loud noises, like the witch and wizard’s argument, could sometimes lead to something good, something kind, something that made the world a little warmer. He didn’t mind so much anymore. He snuggled deeper into his hollow, Pip a warm weight on his chest. He listened to the gentle sounds of the Whispering Woods, feeling safe and sound. A quiet curiosity replaced his old fear.
